impacts.caseName: Teva Pharmaceuticals International GmbH v. Eli Lilly and Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in granting judgment as a matter of law that patent claims directed to using humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies to treat headache were invalid for failure to satisfy the written-description and enablement requirements of 35 U.S.C. § 112.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed JMOL invalidating Teva's headache patents covering methods of using humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies. The court found the claims were adequately supported by the specification, which disclosed known antibodies, known humanization methods, and a representative species. This decision reinstates a jury verdict finding willful infringement by Lilly, potentially impacting competition with Lilly's migraine products.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders in the biopharmaceutical space benefit from the court's recognition that genus claims covering humanized antibodies can satisfy written description and enablement when the specification discloses known starting materials and known methods, reducing the risk of post-verdict JMOL invalidation.
impacts.negativeImplications: Competitors like Lilly face renewed infringement liability and potential damages for products that fall within broad antibody genus claims, even where the patentee disclosed only one specific humanized antibody in the specification.

impacts.caseName: Insulet Corp. v. EOFlow, Co. Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the three-year statute of limitations under the Defend Trade Secrets Act had expired before Insulet brought suit for trade secret misappropriation related to the development of a competing insulin patch pump.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's denial of JMOL, holding that Insulet's DTSA claim was time-barred because Insulet knew or should have known of the misappropriation more than three years before filing suit. The court found that evidence of former employees sharing CAD files and design information in 2018 triggered the statute of limitations well before the 2023 filing. This vacated a jury damages award and permanent injunction.
impacts.positiveImplications: Companies accused of trade secret misappropriation benefit from strict enforcement of the DTSA's three-year statute of limitations, providing a clear defense when the plaintiff delayed filing despite early knowledge of alleged misappropriation.
impacts.negativeImplications: Trade secret owners face significant risk of losing claims if they delay litigation after discovering potential misappropriation; companies must act promptly upon learning that former employees may have shared proprietary information with competitors.

impacts.caseName: Versata Software, LLC v. Ford Motor Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in excluding trade secret damages expert testimony and in overturning a jury's breach of contract damages award in a case involving misappropriation of automotive configuration software.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the trade secret damages judgment and remanded for a new trial, holding the district court improperly excluded two damages models. The court also reversed the district court's post-trial reduction of breach of contract damages and reinstated the jury's award. The case involves Ford's development of competing software after licensing Versata's automotive configuration tools under a master subscription agreement.
impacts.positiveImplications: Software licensors and trade secret owners benefit from the court's broader acceptance of damages methodologies, including models measuring defendant's enrichment, and from the reinstatement of jury contract damages awards.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies that develop in-house alternatives after licensing third-party software face expanded trade secret damages exposure, as courts may permit multiple damages theories at trial including unjust enrichment measures.

impacts.caseName: VLSI Technology LLC v. Intel Corporation
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court correctly granted summary judgment of noninfringement based on extraterritoriality and properly struck a damages expert's theories for inadequate disclosure in damages contentions.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed-in-part Intel's summary judgment of noninfringement of VLSI's multicore processor patent, finding genuine issues of material fact regarding extraterritoriality and doctrine of equivalents. The court affirmed the striking of certain damages theories for failure to adequately disclose them. The case is remanded for further proceedings on infringement of this patent worth potentially billions in damages.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders asserting infringement of semiconductor technology patents benefit from the court's willingness to allow infringement claims to proceed to trial even when manufacturing and design occur partly overseas.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology companies face continued exposure to high-value patent infringement claims, and must carefully monitor opposing parties' damages contentions disclosures to challenge inadequately disclosed theories early.

impacts.caseName: Enanta Pharmaceuticals, Inc. v. Pfizer Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a patent claiming compounds covering nirmatrelvir (Paxlovid's active ingredient) was entitled to priority from a provisional application that contained an alleged typographical error in a chemical substituent definition, and whether the patent was anticipated by Pfizer's intervening public disclosure.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed summary judgment invalidating Enanta's patent covering coronavirus protease inhibitors, holding that the change from 'C2-C12-alkyl' in the provisional to 'C1-C12-alkyl' in the non-provisional application was not an obvious typographical error. Because the patent could not claim priority from the earlier provisional, Pfizer's intervening disclosure of nirmatrelvir anticipated the claims. This eliminates Enanta's infringement claim against Pfizer's blockbuster Paxlovid product.
impacts.positiveImplications: Pfizer and generic manufacturers benefit from the elimination of patent claims that could have restricted competition for COVID-19 treatments, preserving market access for Paxlovid without royalty obligations.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent applicants face heightened risk from errors in provisional applications; a single character discrepancy in a chemical formula can destroy priority claims and expose the patent to anticipation by intervening prior art.

impacts.caseName: Ironburg Inventions Ltd. v. Valve Corporation
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether inter partes review estoppel under 35 U.S.C. § 315(e)(2) barred Valve from asserting two invalidity grounds in district court litigation that were not raised in a prior IPR petition.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's application of IPR estoppel against Valve, holding that the court relied on insufficient evidence for one prior art ground and failed to adequately account for hindsight bias for another. The decision clarifies that the 'reasonably could have raised' standard for IPR estoppel requires rigorous, non-hindsight analysis of whether a skilled searcher would have discovered the prior art.
impacts.positiveImplications: Companies defending against patent infringement claims benefit from the court's narrowing of IPR estoppel, preserving the ability to raise invalidity defenses in district court that were not included in prior IPR petitions.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders relying on IPR estoppel to prevent defendants from raising new invalidity theories at trial face a higher bar to prove that prior art references were reasonably discoverable during the IPR filing window.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to non-uniform constellations for digital communication systems are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court properly denied JMOL on infringement and damages.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the summary judgment of patent eligibility for certain claims of the '761 and '700 patents directed to non-uniform constellations, finding insufficient analysis under Alice, while affirming eligibility for claims of the '509 and '922 patents. The court affirmed the denial of JMOL on non-infringement and damages. The case involves a substantial jury verdict against LG for willful infringement in communications technology used in televisions.
impacts.positiveImplications: The affirmance of eligibility for certain communication technology patents and of the infringement and damages verdicts supports patent holders' ability to monetize innovations in digital signal processing and broadcast technology.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology manufacturers face continued patent eligibility uncertainty, as the court remanded for further § 101 analysis on some claims, and the partial vacatur signals ongoing risk that communication-method patents may be invalidated as abstract ideas.

impacts.caseName: AGI SureTrack LLC v. Farmers Edge Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to automated systems for capturing, processing, and sharing farming data using passive relay devices on farming equipment are patent-ineligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court erred in not finding the case exceptional under § 285.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed that AGI's farming data collection patents are directed to patent-ineligible abstract ideas, but vacated the district court's determination that the case was not exceptional and remanded for reconsideration of attorneys' fees under § 285. The court found that the claims recite conventional data collection and processing steps applied to the farming context without an inventive concept.
impacts.positiveImplications: Agricultural technology companies defending against patent assertions benefit from the invalidation of broad data-collection patents, and the vacatur on exceptionality opens the door for fee awards against weak patent claims.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders in precision agriculture and IoT-related fields face increased § 101 vulnerability for claims that automate data collection and processing, even when directed to specific industrial applications like farming.

impacts.caseName: Ollnova Technologies Ltd. v. ecobee Technologies ULC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred by using a single jury question on infringement covering all asserted patents, by denying § 101 motions for certain building automation patents, and by improperly instructing the jury on the '495 patent's validity under § 101.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the $11.5 million infringement and damages judgment against ecobee and remanded for a new trial, holding that the verdict form's single infringement question covering all four asserted patents was prejudicially erroneous because it prevented meaningful appellate review. The court affirmed that the '887 and '371 patents survive § 101 scrutiny but vacated and remanded on the '495 patent's § 101 analysis under Alice step two.
impacts.positiveImplications: Defendants benefit from the requirement that jury verdict forms separately address infringement for each asserted patent, enabling meaningful post-trial and appellate review of multi-patent cases.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders pursuing multi-patent infringement cases face the risk of retrial if verdict forms aggregate infringement findings across patents, potentially increasing litigation costs and delaying recovery.

impacts.caseName: International Medical Devices, Inc. v. Cornell
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether there was legally sufficient evidence to support the jury's finding that four asserted trade secrets related to cosmetic penile implants were protectable trade secrets under California law, and whether the inventorship challenge to defendants' patents could stand.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the denial of JMOL on trade secret claims, holding that the plaintiff failed to prove the asserted trade secrets qualified as protectable because the underlying concepts were generally known in the art. The court also reversed on patent invalidity for the same reason and vacated the permanent injunction, exemplary damages, and reasonable royalty awards, while affirming liability on a trademark counterfeiting claim.
impacts.positiveImplications: Defendants in trade secret cases benefit from the court's rigorous requirement that plaintiffs prove their claimed secrets are not generally known, establishing a meaningful threshold for trade secret protection.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies relying on trade secret protection face increased risk of losing claims if they cannot clearly demonstrate that the information goes beyond what is generally known in the relevant field, even after a favorable jury verdict.

impacts.caseName: Otsuka America Pharmaceutical, Inc. v. Hetero Labs Limited
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly construed the claim terms 'dextromethorphan' and 'quinidine' in a weight-to-weight ratio limitation for Nuedexta's patent, and whether it erred in waiving the Rule 65(c) bond requirement pending appeal of a preliminary injunction.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the preliminary injunction blocking Hetero's generic competitor to Nuedexta but vacated the district court's waiver of the bond requirement under Rule 65(c). The court held that the claim terms refer to the drugs in any form (including salt forms), supporting Otsuka's infringement theory. The bond vacatur means Otsuka must post security to protect Hetero from losses if the injunction is ultimately reversed.
impacts.positiveImplications: Branded pharmaceutical companies benefit from the claim construction holding that drug compound names in patent claims encompass salt forms, strengthening enforcement against generic ANDA filers.
impacts.negativeImplications: Generic drug companies face barriers to market entry from preliminary injunctions, though the bond requirement provides some financial protection; branded companies must now post bonds even when equities strongly favor injunctive relief.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a Rule 30(b)(6) corporate representative may testify on matters outside their personal knowledge for purposes of establishing the on-sale bar under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. § 102(b), and whether computer source code constitutes hearsay.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed summary judgment of invalidity under the on-sale bar, holding that a 30(b)(6) corporate representative may testify about pre-sale activities even without personal knowledge. The court also held that computer source code is not hearsay because executable commands are not 'statements' under the Federal Rules of Evidence. These rulings facilitated proof that a prior art device was sold more than one year before the patent's priority date.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from expanded evidentiary tools to prove invalidity, including the use of 30(b)(6) testimony about historical corporate activities and admission of source code without hearsay objections.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face greater invalidity risk from on-sale bar challenges, as corporate designees can testify about pre-critical-date sales without personal knowledge and source code is freely admissible as non-hearsay evidence.

impacts.caseName: A.L.M. Holding Company v. Zydex Industries Private Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a patent owner that retained the right to sue for infringement while granting an exclusive license to manufacture and sell had sufficient constitutional standing to bring a patent infringement suit.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's dismissal for lack of standing, holding that a patent owner who retains an exclusionary right to sue third parties for infringement—even after granting an exclusive license to commercialize—possesses sufficient injury-in-fact to satisfy Article III standing. The court found the retained right to sue was not rendered illusory by the license terms.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners who license commercialization rights but retain enforcement rights benefit from the clarity that retained exclusionary rights are sufficient for standing, enabling flexible licensing structures that preserve litigation authority.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers cannot easily challenge standing by pointing to exclusive licenses; the decision narrows the grounds on which licensee-based standing challenges can succeed when the licensor retains the right to sue.

impacts.caseName: Federal Express Corporation v. Qualcomm Incorporated
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Board's obviousness determination was supported by substantial evidence where a non-party to the underlying district court litigation filed IPR petitions challenging the same patents on the petitioner's filing deadline, and whether such third-party IPR petitions raise procedural concerns.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the Board's finding that FedEx's sensor-based logistics patent claims were unpatentable as obvious and remanded for further proceedings. The court noted the unusual circumstance that Qualcomm, a non-party to the underlying district court litigation, filed IPR petitions challenging FedEx's patents on the final day that the actual defendant could have filed. The decision raises important questions about third-party IPR petitions potentially filed as proxies.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners benefit from the court's heightened scrutiny of IPR petitions filed by non-parties that appear strategically timed to coincide with a defendant's filing deadline, potentially limiting abuse of the IPR system.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies that rely on third parties to challenge competitor patents through IPR proceedings face increased procedural risk and scrutiny, potentially undermining strategic use of the IPR system.

impacts.caseName: TrackTime, LLC v. Amazon.com Services LLC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether claim terms reciting 'executable program code configured to' perform specified functions should be construed as means-plus-function limitations under 35 U.S.C. § 112(f) in light of intervening precedent in Dyfan, LLC v. Target Corp.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the district court's indefiniteness ruling invalidating the '978 patent and remanded for reconsideration under the Dyfan framework, which issued after the district court's original ruling. The court held that whether 'executable program code configured to' invokes § 112(f) requires further analysis under the updated precedent. The court separately affirmed invalidity of a '638 patent claim for anticipation.
impacts.positiveImplications: Software patent holders benefit from the court's willingness to reconsider means-plus-function determinations under evolving precedent, potentially rescuing claims from indefiniteness rulings based on outdated legal standards.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology companies defending against software patent assertions face uncertainty as the scope of § 112(f) for 'configured to' claim terms remains unsettled, potentially prolonging litigation on remand.
